summary: Specifies ways to communicate route exclusions when setting up paths with RSVP-TE. It builds on RFC 3209 and the GMPLS extensions of RFC 3473, which allow explicit route hints, and lets a requester say which nodes or links the path must avoid. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP-TE path requests can name places a route should include, but they also need a way to name places it must avoid. This RFC adds whole-path and segment-specific exclusion lists for routers that build the route.

subtitle: RSVP-TE path requests can list nodes, links, and shared risks that a route must avoid.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE can say which nodes or resources a path should include, but not which it must avoid. Routers that expand a partial route may need exclusion information to build a diverse path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an EXCLUDE_ROUTE object for exclusions across a whole path and an Explicit Exclusion Route subobject for exclusions between two route hops. Both can identify Shared Risk Link Groups.
tldr.outcome: Routers can account for required exclusions while expanding a route, including when setting up a protection path. RFC 4874 updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 and was updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 8390.

today: RFC 4874 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473. It has also been updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 8390.

sections.title: Why a Path Request Needs an Exclusion List
sections.content:
The Resource Reservation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) uses an Explicit Route Object (ERO) to identify nodes and resources to include in a path. It did not provide a matching way to signal nodes or resources to exclude.

This matters when the head-end does not compute the complete route. A later router may expand a loose hop or abstract node and needs to avoid part of an existing route. The RFC describes using exclusions to build non-overlapping Label Switched Paths (LSPs).

It defines a whole-path Exclude Route list and a separate exclusion that applies only between two abstract nodes named in an ERO.
sections.plainLanguage: A route request can name required waypoints, but routers also need to know which resources to avoid. This RFC adds a whole-path avoid list and a list for one part of a path.

sections.title: Exclusions Constrain Route Selection
sections.content:
An exclusion is intended to constrain normal route selection, not to spell out every possible hop that a route must avoid. The RFC recommends signaling only the minimum useful set of items, such as the Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs) that a backup path should avoid.

In a path that crosses several computation domains, a router can remove exclusion entries once they no longer affect later route expansion. The RFC's example removes entries as the path crosses area boundaries, while retaining information needed by the next router.

Implementations should also consider the size of the signaled data and its effect on RSVP signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The exclusion list should carry only the information needed to constrain route choices. Routers may remove entries after those entries no longer affect the remaining path.

sections.title: The EXCLUDE_ROUTE Object
sections.content:
The EXCLUDE_ROUTE object (XRO) carries a list of abstract nodes or resources to avoid on the LSP's path. It uses class 232 and C_Type 1. Its variable-length subobjects can identify IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes, unnumbered interfaces, Autonomous Systems, or SRLGs.

The XRO reuses an L bit to distinguish a required exclusion from a preference. A zero means the item MUST be excluded; a one means it SHOULD be avoided, but the path may use it if necessary. Address and interface subobjects also have an Attribute field that can identify an interface, a whole node, or the SRLGs associated with an interface.

The new SRLG subobject has type 34, length 8, and a 32-bit SRLG identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The XRO carries identifiers for nodes, interfaces, address ranges, or shared-risk groups that a path should avoid. Each entry says whether avoidance is mandatory or preferred.

sections.title: How Routers Apply the XRO
sections.content:
A router checks whether it belongs to an excluded abstract node and whether a resource it would use belongs to an excluded SRLG. If an exclusion conflicts with an ERO entry, an XRO item marked for mandatory exclusion takes precedence and the router rejects the Path message.

When selecting a next hop or expanding the route, a router must not add a node, link, or resource that a mandatory XRO entry excludes. It should minimize use of entries marked only as avoid. A router may reject a list that is too complex under local policy and return an XRO Too Complex error.

The XRO class number allows a router that does not understand the object to forward it without examining it. A supporting router may remove entries that no longer matter, but it must not put the same node in both the XRO and the ERO.
sections.plainLanguage: Each capable router checks the exclusion list before choosing or expanding the next route segment. It must honor required exclusions and can report a list that is too complex to process.

sections.title: Explicit Exclusions Between Route Hops
sections.content:
The Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS), type 33, is carried inside an ERO. It contains one or more exclusion subobjects in the same formats used by an XRO, but its scope is limited to the path between the preceding and following abstract nodes in the ERO.

A router applies the XRO processing rules to an EXRS within that segment. If the XRO and EXRS both apply, the router must honor both; where they disagree, the stricter request wins. A node that does not support EXRS handles it as an unknown ERO subobject.

An implementation must support XRO. EXRS support is optional. The RFC sets minimum support requirements for IPv4 and IPv6 prefix subobjects.
sections.plainLanguage: An EXRS places an exclusion inside the route and limits it to one segment between two named hops. Routers apply the same exclusion rules used for the whole-path list.

sections.title: Using Exclusions for Protection Paths
sections.content:
The appendix shows how an ingress can set up a backup LSP that avoids nodes or links used by a primary LSP. In an inter-area path, later area-border routers use the remaining exclusion entries while expanding their part of the route, then remove entries that no longer matter.

For inter-AS protection, an exclusion list can carry the primary route when the backup follows a different AS path. SRLG identifiers are useful across AS boundaries only when the ASes share a consistent identifier space; otherwise, the entering AS border router can translate a link address into local SRLG identifiers.

The RFC also describes use in an optical-core overlay and in a single area where the routing information does not include traffic-engineering extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup path can use the primary path's recorded nodes, links, or risk groups as exclusions. Routers then use those exclusions while calculating each part of the backup route.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new messages or substantial processing, so the security considerations of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 continue to apply. A network boundary that removes explicit routes from Path messages should also consider whether it must remove the XRO.

A very large or complex XRO or EXRS could cause extra processing at each router and be used for denial of service. A router may reject an exclusion list that exceeds its local limits.
sections.plainLanguage: A very complex exclusion list can make routers do extra work. The RFC allows a router to reject a list that exceeds its local limits.
